runs.latest_final: The narrator's younger sister is genuinely dead and was already dead when the narrator came home, where they lived together. Her death was not a suicide, and it was not a killing by the narrator or by another person, nor an accident the narrator caused. The narrator deliberately wrote a note intended to be read as the dead sister's own suicide note, so that people—including the third person they lived with—would believe the sister had died by suicide. The note was easy to write because its text described the narrator's own wish to die: the narrator projected their own suicidal feelings onto the dead sister. The deception was not for money, not to protect anyone, not to cover a murder, and the narrator was not forced. The motive is tied to the narrator's own death wish—the note recasts the sister's non-suicidal death as a chosen suicide, mirroring the narrator's own desire to die—while also shaping how the death is perceived and officially treated.

runs.latest_final: The man borrows books for his child, who cannot go to the library. The child has a habit of writing his or her own name on page 30 of every library book the child reads. The man knows this habit. Before choosing a book, he opens it to page 30 and looks for the child's name. If the name is there, the child has already read that book, so he does not borrow it. If the name is not there, the book is new to the child, and he borrows it to take home so the child has something fresh to read. The man checks page 30 because that is where the child always writes his or her name.
